之禮以通上下之情此天保荅君之詩所由作
也噫君燕其臣臣媚其君周室君臣共成一代
光明之業而均享治安之福也有由然歟
維仲山甫柔亦不茹剛亦不吐
錢俊民
同考試官訓導寸司馬 批 講不茹不吐及兩亦字
皆有思致吉甫作誦之意此作庶幾盡之
同考試官教授陳 批 剛柔不偏正山甫柔嘉
維則處作者多不能道此卷直以數語抑揚之而其義意自見
punctuated:
君之福方興而未艾，如川之始至而不可量者，盖必增之而又增，無終窮也。其興也孰加焉？源源不竭，浩然而不可測者，川之方来也。我后之福日進而無疆，如川之方来而不可限者，盖必益之而復益，無止極也。其盛也孰尚焉？噫！期君福於無窮，寓忠愛於罔極，臣子厚報其君之意，固如是哉！抑論之，朝廷之禮以敬為主，君臣之分以嚴為主。然一於嚴敬而情或不通，則上下不交，而德業之成也難矣。故先王制為燕饗之禮，以通上下之情，此《天保》荅君之詩所由作也。噫！君燕其臣，臣媚其君，周室君臣共成一代光明之業，而均享治安之福也，有由然歟！
維仲山甫，柔亦不茹，剛亦不吐。
錢俊民
同考試官訓導寸司馬批：講不茹不吐及兩亦字，皆有思致。吉甫作誦之意，此作庶幾盡之。
同考試官教授陳批：剛柔不偏，正山甫柔嘉維則處。作者多不能道，此卷直以數語抑揚之，而其義意自見。
translation_en:
…The ruler’s blessings are just beginning to rise and show no sign of ceasing. Like a river’s first surge, they cannot be measured: surely they will increase and increase again, without end. What could surpass their rising? Flowing on inexhaustibly, vast and unfathomable—such is a river as it comes onward. Our sovereign’s blessings advance daily without bounds. Like the onward flow of a river, they cannot be confined: surely they will grow and grow again, without limit. What could exceed their abundance? Ah! To wish the ruler blessings without end and to lodge one’s loyal affection in what knows no bounds—such indeed is the intention of a subject seeking to repay his ruler generously!
To consider this further: reverence is fundamental to court ritual, and strictness is fundamental to the distinction between ruler and subject. Yet if strictness and reverence alone prevail, and feelings sometimes fail to pass between them, those above and below will have no communication, and achievement in virtue and governance will be difficult. Thus the former kings instituted the rites of banqueting and feasting to allow the feelings of those above and below to communicate. This is why “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), the poem answering the ruler, was composed. Ah! The ruler feasted his subjects, and the subjects showed affection for their ruler. That the rulers and subjects of the Zhou house together accomplished the illustrious achievements of an age and shared equally in the blessings of peace and good order surely had its reasons!
“As for Zhong Shanfu, the soft he does not devour, nor does he spit out the hard.”
Qian Junmin
Comment by Associate Examiner, Instructor Cun Sima [?]: His exposition of “does not devour” and “does not spit out,” and of both occurrences of “nor” (yi), shows thoughtful insight throughout. This composition comes close to fully expressing Jifu’s intention in composing his song of praise.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Professor Chen: Being partial neither toward the hard nor toward the soft is precisely where Shanfu’s gentle goodness serves as a model. Most writers cannot articulate this. This essay brings it out through the measured rise and fall of just a few phrases, and the meaning reveals itself…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
見是可與言詩矣
考試官左中允楊批〔得詩人言外之意〕
考試官右諭德王批〔作大雅義當如此〕
詩人美大臣既不因人之弱以示強亦不因人
之強以示弱盖柔嘉之德人所難全也大臣柔
不茹而剛不吐此其所以獨異於人也歟昔宣
王命樊侯仲山甫築城于齊而尹吉甫作詩以
送之至此盖謂內之慊者必隨物而有遷德之
備者不因人而少變彼柔則茹之人雖有是言
===
也維我仲山甫則柔亦不茹焉剛則吐之人言
固如是也維我仲山甫則剛亦不吐焉是故人
之柔者委靡而無特立之操退縮而無兼人之
勇是其可欺猶物之柔脆者可茹也山甫以為
彼柔而我茹之我若侮其柔矣於是遇之以禮
懷之以仁優容之以引其不及俯就之以矜其
不能柔者其肯茹之乎若夫人之剛者恃血氣
之強以陵乎弱挾粗暴之氣以加于人是其不
可犯猶物之堅韌者必吐也山甫以為彼剛而
punctuated:
見，是可與言詩矣。
考試官左中允楊批〔得詩人言外之意〕。
考試官右諭德王批〔作大雅義當如此〕。
詩人美大臣既不因人之弱以示強，亦不因人之強以示弱。盖柔嘉之德，人所難全也。大臣柔不茹而剛不吐，此其所以獨異於人也歟！昔宣王命樊侯仲山甫築城于齊，而尹吉甫作詩以送之。至此，盖謂內之慊者必隨物而有遷，德之備者不因人而少變。彼柔則茹之，人雖有是言也，維我仲山甫則柔亦不茹焉；剛則吐之，人言固如是也，維我仲山甫則剛亦不吐焉。是故人之柔者，委靡而無特立之操，退縮而無兼人之勇，是其可欺，猶物之柔脆者可茹也。山甫以為彼柔而我茹之，我若侮其柔矣。於是遇之以禮，懷之以仁，優容之以引其不及，俯就之以矜其不能。柔者，其肯茹之乎？若夫人之剛者，恃血氣之強以陵乎弱，挾粗暴之氣以加于人，是其不可犯，猶物之堅韌者必吐也。山甫以為彼剛而
translation_en:
…is apparent; this is someone with whom one can discuss the Odes.
Examiner Yang, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent, comments: 〔Captures the poet’s meaning beyond his words.〕
Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent, comments: 〔This is how an exposition of the Greater Odes should be written.〕
The poet praises a great minister who neither displays strength because others are weak nor displays weakness because others are strong. Gentle goodness is a virtue that people find difficult to possess in full. This great minister neither swallows the soft nor spits out the hard: is this not what sets him apart from others?
Formerly, King Xuan commanded Zhong Shanfu, Marquis of Fan, to build a wall at Qi, and Yin Jifu composed a poem to see him off. At this point, his meaning is that those deficient within inevitably shift with external circumstances, whereas those complete in virtue do not change even slightly on account of others. Although people say, “Swallow what is soft,” our Zhong Shanfu does not swallow even the soft. Although people indeed say, “Spit out what is hard,” our Zhong Shanfu does not spit out even the hard.
Thus, weak people are dispirited and lack the integrity to stand independently; they shrink back and lack courage surpassing that of others. They can therefore be bullied, just as soft, brittle things can be swallowed. Shanfu considers: “If they are weak and I swallow them, I would be insulting their weakness.” Accordingly, he treats them with propriety, cherishes them with benevolence, generously accommodates them to help them overcome their shortcomings, and stoops to meet them out of compassion for their incapacity. Would he be willing to swallow the weak?
As for the strong, they rely on their physical vigor to oppress the weak and bring their coarse, violent temper to bear upon others. They cannot therefore be challenged, just as hard, tough things must be spat out. Shanfu considers: “If they are strong and…”

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
我吐之我亦不為剛矣於是制之以威待之以
嚴頓挫之使其強不得肆摧拉之使其勢不得
張剛者其肯吐之乎吁柔亦不茹是遇剛者則
然非偏於柔也剛亦不吐是遇柔者則然非不
能剛也以此觀之則山甫之柔嘉非軟美之謂
而其所以保身者亦可知矣抑又論之天生烝
民有物有則不吐不茹剛柔之則也此盖衆人
稟性受氣之所同者而獨歸之山甫何哉盖山
甫鍾氣之秀而全德之美者故其柔嘉維則至
===
於如此然其學問進修之功亦有不可誣者此
其所以優于城齊之行而為中興之良佐也吉
甫喜談而樂道之其真好是懿德者邪
春秋
齊侯宋公江人黃人盟于貫僖公二年楚
人伐黃僖公十一年
宋鏜
同考試官教諭劉 批此題自有兩傳塲中主伐黃
者頗多獨此卷參用之可取
punctuated:
我吐之，我亦不為剛矣。於是制之以威，待之以嚴，頓挫之使其強不得肆，摧拉之使其勢不得張。剛者其肯吐之乎？吁！柔亦不茹，是遇剛者則然，非偏於柔也；剛亦不吐，是遇柔者則然，非不能剛也。以此觀之，則山甫之柔嘉非軟美之謂，而其所以保身者亦可知矣。抑又論之，天生烝民，有物有則。不吐不茹，剛柔之則也。此盖衆人稟性受氣之所同者，而獨歸之山甫，何哉？盖山甫鍾氣之秀而全德之美者，故其柔嘉維則至於如此。然其學問進修之功，亦有不可誣者。此其所以優于城齊之行，而為中興之良佐也。吉甫喜談而樂道之，其真好是懿德者邪？

春秋
齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人盟于貫，僖公二年。楚人伐黃，僖公十一年。
宋鏜
同考試官教諭劉批：此題自有兩傳，塲中主伐黃者頗多，獨此卷參用之，可取。
translation_en:
…if I spit him out, then I too cannot be considered firm. Thus he restrains such a man with authority and treats him with severity, checking him so that his strength cannot run unchecked, breaking his resistance so that his power cannot expand. Would he be willing to spit out the strong?

Ah! He does not devour the soft: this is how he acts when encountering the strong [?], rather than being partial to softness. He does not spit out the hard: this is how he acts when encountering the soft [?], rather than being incapable of firmness. Viewed in this light, Shanfu’s gentleness and goodness do not mean pliant agreeableness, and we can also understand how he preserves himself.

Let us consider this further. Heaven gives birth to the multitude of the people; for every thing there is a governing norm. Neither spitting out nor devouring is the norm governing firmness and gentleness. This is surely something all people share in their endowed nature and vital energy. Why, then, is it attributed to Shanfu alone? Shanfu concentrated within himself the finest vital energy and possessed the beauty of complete virtue; hence his exemplary gentleness and goodness reached such a degree. Yet the contribution of his learning and continued self-cultivation likewise cannot be denied. This is why he surpassed the conduct described as “cheng qi” [?] and became an excellent assistant in the dynastic restoration. Jifu delighted in speaking of him and gladly praised him: was he truly one who loved this admirable virtue?

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and men of Jiang and Huang made a covenant at Guan.” Second year of Duke Xi.
“Men of Chu attacked Huang.” Eleventh year of Duke Xi.

Song Tang

Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: This topic has two commentarial accounts. Among the candidates in the examination hall, quite a few concentrated on the attack on Huang. This paper alone draws on both accounts and is worthy of selection.

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官左中允楊批善叙事不失胡傳之旨
考試官右諭德王批詞嚴義正
霸主得交遠之謀春秋善其始霸主失卹遠之
義春秋罪其終此江黃貫澤之盟與楚人伐黃
之役齊桓之得失自不能相掩也且楚自春秋
以来已為中國之患積其吞併之力至是又五
十年此齊桓之所為隱憂焉者然意其有與國
之助也於是始為貫澤之盟以修江黃之好凡
我友邦共伸安夏之義及此遠國同宣攘楚之
===
威雖曰君子屢盟亂是用長盟非美事也而桓
之名則正矣楚人聞之必將私語於其國曰齊
其已服江黃乎右臂之援我以之失掎角之勢
彼以之成矣自是而齊之霸業遂振或為陘亭
之次或為召陵之盟皆今日權輿之也是不亦
得交遠之謀哉故春秋書曰齊侯宋公江人黃
人盟于貫諸侯皆在而獨言遠國者許其能服
江黃也夫黃自受盟以後遂廢楚人之貢計其
利害之間相去且九百里此楚人之所欲甘心
punctuated:
考試官左中允楊批：善叙事，不失胡傳之旨。

考試官右諭德王批：詞嚴義正。

霸主得交遠之謀，春秋善其始；霸主失卹遠之義，春秋罪其終。此江黃貫澤之盟與楚人伐黃之役，齊桓之得失自不能相掩也。且楚自春秋以来，已為中國之患，積其吞併之力，至是又五十年，此齊桓之所為隱憂焉者。然意其有與國之助也，於是始為貫澤之盟，以修江黃之好。凡我友邦，共伸安夏之義；及此遠國，同宣攘楚之威。雖曰「君子屢盟，亂是用長」，盟非美事也，而桓之名則正矣。楚人聞之，必將私語於其國曰：「齊其已服江黃乎？右臂之援，我以之失；掎角之勢，彼以之成矣。」自是而齊之霸業遂振，或為陘亭之次，或為召陵之盟，皆今日權輿之也。是不亦得交遠之謀哉？故春秋書曰：「齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人盟于貫。」諸侯皆在，而獨言遠國者，許其能服江黃也。夫黃自受盟以後，遂廢楚人之貢，計其利害之間，相去且九百里，此楚人之所欲甘心
translation_en:
Examiner Yang, Left Mentor, comments: “The narrative is well handled and remains faithful to the purport of Hu’s Commentary.”

Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher, comments: “The language is stern and the principles correct.”

When the hegemon devised a sound strategy for establishing relations with distant states, the Spring and Autumn Annals commended his beginning; when the hegemon failed in his duty to protect distant states, the Spring and Autumn Annals condemned his end. Thus, in the covenant with Jiang and Huang at Guanze and the campaign in which the men of Chu attacked Huang, Duke Huan of Qi’s successes and failures cannot conceal one another. Ever since the beginning of the Spring and Autumn period, Chu had been a menace to the Central States. By this time, another fifty years had passed during which it had accumulated strength through annexation. This was what secretly troubled Duke Huan of Qi. Yet he thought that he could obtain assistance from allied states. He therefore first concluded the covenant at Guanze to cultivate friendship with Jiang and Huang. All our friendly states would together uphold the duty of securing the Xia states; joined by these distant states, they would together display their might in repelling Chu. Although it is said, “When gentlemen repeatedly make covenants, disorder thereby grows,” and covenant-making is no admirable affair, Duke Huan’s declared purpose was nevertheless legitimate.

When the men of Chu heard of this, they must have said privately within their state: “Has Qi already brought Jiang and Huang into submission? Through this we have lost the support of our right arm, while they have established a position from which to attack us on two sides.” From this point Qi’s hegemony flourished. Whether the encampment at Xingting or the covenant at Shaoling, all had their beginnings in this day’s undertaking. Was this not a sound strategy for establishing relations with distant states? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals records: “The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and men of Jiang and Huang covenanted at Guan.” The feudal lords were all present, yet the particular mention of the distant states acknowledges his ability to bring Jiang and Huang into submission.

After Huang entered into the covenant, it ceased paying tribute to Chu. In weighing the advantages and dangers, [it reckoned that] the distance separating them was nearly nine hundred li [?]. This was what made the men of Chu wish to satisfy their resentment …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
由叫始則四國舉兵而同會繼則我公與會而
同盟倒持太阿授楚其柄孰知諸夏親暱之不
可棄戎狄豺狼之不可厭邪故春秋於楚書人
而諸侯書爵傳曰人楚子所以人諸侯又書諸
侯盟于宋而我公之罪亦於是乎著矣詩曰戎
狄是膺荆舒是懲又曰奮伐荆楚深入其阻列
國昧焉至若楚雖得曹新昏於衛然其君不在
會其師不與圍故方之諸國非有從夷之罪也
特以晋文出亡於曹則有觀祼之恥於衛則有
===
與塊之辱此直睚眦之怨何足以介懷也為晋
文謀者惟宜存反仁反禮之心誦懲忿窒慾之
戒擴公恕之量止貪憤之兵可也夫何念不及
此始焉潜師以侵曹徑入其國都而不顧忽焉
揚聲以伐衛雖其君請盟而弗許忿不思難惟
怨是圖孰知楚人假被髮纓冠之義而有恤患
救難之舉邪故春秋於侵曹伐衛再稱晋侯傳
曰譏復怨也又書楚人救衛而晋文之罪於是
乎深矣詩云不忮不求何用不臧書云必有忍
punctuated:
由叫，始則四國舉兵而同會，繼則我公與會而同盟，倒持太阿，授楚其柄。孰知諸夏親暱之不可棄，戎狄豺狼之不可厭邪？故《春秋》於楚書人，而諸侯書爵。傳曰：「人楚子，所以人諸侯。」又書諸侯盟于宋，而我公之罪亦於是乎著矣。《詩》曰：「戎狄是膺，荆舒是懲。」又曰：「奮伐荆楚，深入其阻。」列國昧焉。
至若楚雖得曹，新昏於衛，然其君不在會，其師不與圍，故方之諸國，非有從夷之罪也。特以晋文出亡，於曹則有觀祼之恥，於衛則有與塊之辱，此直睚眦之怨，何足以介懷也？為晋文謀者，惟宜存反仁反禮之心，誦懲忿窒慾之戒，擴公恕之量，止貪憤之兵可也。夫何念不及此，始焉潜師以侵曹，徑入其國都而不顧；忽焉揚聲以伐衛，雖其君請盟而弗許。忿不思難，惟怨是圖，孰知楚人假被髮纓冠之義，而有恤患救難之舉邪？故《春秋》於侵曹伐衛再稱晋侯。傳曰：「譏復怨也。」又書楚人救衛，而晋文之罪於是乎深矣。《詩》云：「不忮不求，何用不臧？」《書》云：「必有忍
translation_en:
…[Opening characters unclear: 由叫.] At first, the four states raised troops and assembled together; afterward, our duke attended the meeting and joined their covenant. This was to hold the sword Tai’a backward and hand its hilt to Chu. Who understood that the close bonds among the Xia states must not be abandoned, and that the wolfish Rong and Di could never be satiated? Thus the Spring and Autumn Annals calls the ruler of Chu a mere “man,” while recording the other feudal lords by their ranks. The Commentary says: “To call the Viscount of Chu a ‘man’ is thereby to treat the other feudal lords as mere ‘men.’” It further records that the feudal lords covenanted at Song, and thus our duke’s guilt also becomes manifest. The Book of Odes says: “Strike down the Rong and Di; chastise Jing and Shu.” It also says: “Vigorously attack Jing-Chu; penetrate deep into its fastnesses.” The various states failed to understand this.
As for Chu, although it had won over Cao and recently formed a marriage alliance with Wei [?], the rulers of those states had not attended the meeting, and their armies had not participated in the siege. Compared with the other states, therefore, they were not guilty of following the barbarians. It was merely that, during Duke Wen of Jin’s exile, he had suffered the humiliation of being watched while naked in Cao and the insult of being given a clod of earth in Wei. These were no more than petty personal grudges. Why should he have taken them to heart? Those advising Duke Wen of Jin ought only to have urged him to examine his own benevolence and ritual propriety, recite the admonition to restrain anger and curb desire, enlarge his capacity for impartiality and forbearance, and halt warfare driven by greed and resentment. Why did his thoughts fail to reach this? First he secretly sent troops to invade Cao, proceeding straight into its capital without scruple. Then he ostentatiously announced an attack on Wei, refusing even its ruler’s request for a covenant. In his anger he gave no thought to the difficulties that might follow, intent only on avenging his grievances. Who realized that the men of Chu would invoke the righteous duty of rushing to another’s aid, with hair unbound and cap hastily tied on, and take action to relieve distress and rescue those in peril? Thus, in recording the invasion of Cao and the attack on Wei, the Spring and Autumn Annals twice names the Marquis of Jin. The Commentary says: “This censures the avenging of a grudge.” It further records that the men of Chu rescued Wei, thereby making Duke Wen of Jin’s guilt still graver. The Book of Odes says: “Neither envious nor grasping—how could he fail to be good?” The Book of Documents says: “There must be forbearance…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□乃有濟有容德乃大晉文愧焉噫諸侯背華
即夷也而罪之均霸主懷私報怨也而罪之甚
聖人致謹於夷夏公私之辨也其嚴乎雖然圍
宋盟宋諸侯之罪固難逃也而鹿上之盟伊誰
之過侵曹伐衞晉文之罪固可譏也而一戰勝
楚遂主夏盟伊誰之功即是而觀則宋襄之過
晉文之功各不相掩矣此又讀經者之所當知
禮記
是故養世子不可不慎也
姚孜
===
同考試官教諭唐批此題作者拘於本文主意
講養世子處多充拓不去此篇能融會經文中大意以發其
義蓋不逐時好者宜取之以冠本房
考試官左中允楊批如此講方見養之慎處
考試官右諭德王批養世子之法亦畧具於此矣
先王之教儲君而必致其謹焉蓋豫教世子人
君之先務也苟教之而不致其謹又何以成其
德哉記禮者記三王之教世子而言及於此意
punctuated:
□乃有濟，有容德乃大。」晉文愧焉。噫！諸侯背華即夷也，而罪之均；霸主懷私報怨也，而罪之甚。聖人致謹於夷夏公私之辨也，其嚴乎！雖然，圍宋、盟宋，諸侯之罪固難逃也，而鹿上之盟，伊誰之過？侵曹、伐衞，晉文之罪固可譏也，而一戰勝楚，遂主夏盟，伊誰之功？即是而觀，則宋襄之過、晉文之功，各不相掩矣。此又讀經者之所當知。
禮記
是故養世子不可不慎也。
姚孜
同考試官教諭唐批：此題作者拘於本文主意，講養世子處，多充拓不去。此篇能融會經文中大意以發其義，蓋不逐時好者，宜取之以冠本房。
考試官左中允楊批：如此講，方見養之慎處。
考試官右諭德王批：養世子之法，亦畧具於此矣。
先王之教儲君，而必致其謹焉。蓋豫教世子，人君之先務也。苟教之而不致其謹，又何以成其德哉？記禮者記三王之教世子，而言及於此意。
translation_en:
…[illegible] then there will be success; with tolerance, virtue becomes great.” Duke Wen of Jin should feel ashamed before these words. Alas! When the regional lords turn their backs on the Hua and join the Yi, they are equally condemned; when the hegemon harbors selfish motives and avenges grievances, he is condemned more severely. How stringent the Sage is in carefully distinguishing Yi from Xia, and public duty from private interest! Nevertheless, although the regional lords cannot escape blame for besieging Song and making a covenant with Song, whose fault was the covenant at Lushang? Although Duke Wen of Jin deserves censure for invading Cao and attacking Wei, whose achievement was it to defeat Chu in a single battle and thereby assume leadership of the Xia alliance? Viewed in this light, Duke Xiang of Song’s fault and Duke Wen of Jin’s achievement cannot obscure one another. This, too, is something readers of the Classic should understand.
Record of Rites
“Therefore, one cannot be other than careful in nurturing the heir apparent.”
Yao Zi
Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, an Instructor: Those who write on this topic are constrained by the main purport of the original passage. In discussing the nurturing of the heir apparent, they generally cannot develop the argument further. This essay integrates the broad meaning of the canonical text to elucidate its significance. Since it does not chase current fashions, it deserves to be selected as the best in this examination section.
Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Only when it is explained in this way does the care required in nurturing become apparent.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent: The methods of nurturing the heir apparent are also broadly set out here.
When the former kings educated the heir apparent, they invariably exercised the utmost care. Indeed, educating the heir apparent in advance is a ruler’s foremost duty. If he educates him without exercising the utmost care, how can he bring his virtue to completion? The recorder of the rites recorded how the kings of the Three Dynasties educated their heirs apparent, and his discussion reached this point.

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
謂世子國家之主器天下之大本將以承宗祧
之重者在是而養之不可以無素將以為社稷
之主者在是而教之不可以不豫是故知為人
子然後可以為人父故君之於世子必盡父道
以養之知為人臣然後可以為人君故君之於
世子必盡君道以教之禮以修其外堅定其德
性樂以修其内消融其邪慝而所以養之之道
無一不致其謹曷敢惑以異端邪太傅在於前
少傅在於後其入則有保其出則有師而所以
===
養之之人無一不極其慎庸敢雜以邪佞邪欲
其明文武之道必春夏學干戈秋冬學羽籥而
養正之功無時而或間也忽慢云乎哉欲其知
長幼之序必養老於東序讓齒於國學而育德
之教無處而不然也苟簡云乎哉吁人君之養
世子如此其慎此所以大善備而克負荷於他
日也歟嗟夫天下之命懸於世子世子之善在
於蚤諭教古之明君有見乎此故為之擇方正
敦良之士以為保傅師友朝夕與之游處左右
punctuated: 謂世子，國家之主器，天下之大本，將以承宗祧之重者在是，而養之不可以無素；將以為社稷之主者在是，而教之不可以不豫。是故知為人子，然後可以為人父，故君之於世子，必盡父道以養之；知為人臣，然後可以為人君，故君之於世子，必盡君道以教之。禮以修其外，堅定其德性；樂以修其内，消融其邪慝。而所以養之之道，無一不致其謹，曷敢惑以異端邪？太傅在於前，少傅在於後，其入則有保，其出則有師。而所以養之之人，無一不極其慎，庸敢雜以邪佞邪？欲其明文武之道，必春夏學干戈，秋冬學羽籥，而養正之功，無時而或間也，忽慢云乎哉？欲其知長幼之序，必養老於東序，讓齒於國學，而育德之教，無處而不然也，苟簡云乎哉？吁！人君之養世子，如此其慎，此所以大善備而克負荷於他日也歟！嗟夫！天下之命懸於世子，世子之善在於蚤諭教。古之明君有見乎此，故為之擇方正敦良之士，以為保傅師友，朝夕與之游處，左右
translation_en:
…means that the heir apparent is the guardian of the state’s sacred vessels and the great foundation of all under Heaven. It is he who will bear the weighty responsibility of continuing the ancestral sacrifices, so his nurture must have a longstanding foundation; it is he who will become lord of the altars of soil and grain, so his instruction must begin in advance. Thus, only after knowing how to be a son can one become a father; therefore, in nurturing the heir apparent, the ruler must fully discharge a father’s duties. Only after knowing how to be a minister can one become a ruler; therefore, in teaching the heir apparent, the ruler must fully discharge a ruler’s duties. Ritual cultivates his outward conduct and strengthens his moral nature; music cultivates his inner being and dissolves his wicked impulses. Every method of nurturing him is thus applied with the utmost care. How could anyone dare confuse him with heterodox teachings? The Grand Preceptor stands before him, and the Junior Preceptor behind him. When he enters, he has a guardian; when he goes out, he has a teacher. Every person charged with nurturing him is thus selected with the utmost care. How could anyone dare admit the wicked and sycophantic among them?

To make him understand the Way of Kings Wen and Wu, he must learn the dances with shields and spears in spring and summer, and those with feathers and flutes in autumn and winter. The work of nurturing his rectitude is never interrupted. How could there be neglect or indifference? To make him understand the proper order of elder and younger, he must honor and nourish the aged in the Eastern School and yield precedence to his elders in the state school. There is no place where instruction that nurtures virtue is not practiced. How could there be carelessness or perfunctoriness? Ah! Such is the care with which a ruler nurtures the heir apparent. Is this not why every great virtue is made complete in him, enabling him to shoulder his responsibilities in days to come?

Alas! The fate of all under Heaven hangs upon the heir apparent, and the goodness of the heir apparent depends upon early guidance and instruction. The enlightened rulers of antiquity understood this. They therefore selected upright, honorable, sincere, and good men to serve as his guardians, preceptors, teachers, and friends, keeping company with him morning and evening. To his left and right…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
前後無非正人出入起居罔非正道則所見者
正事所聞者正言所行者正道而世子正矣先
儒曰太子正而天下定此天下之至言萬世不
可易之定論也
天高地下萬物散殊而禮制行矣流而不
息合同而化而樂興焉
李岫
同考試官教諭唐批有天地之和序而後有禮樂
之制作作者往往認天地之和序為禮樂失之矣此篇獨得
===
其大意故表而出之
考試官左中允楊批講禮行樂興處最是
考試官右諭德王批體認親切
造化示自然之序而禮所由制造化示自然之
和而樂所由作夫高下散殊者天地自然之序
而周流同化者天地自然之和也孰謂禮樂之
制作而有外於是哉今夫天尊於上地卑於下
一高一下而兩儀之位定矣大以成大小以成小
有大有小而萬物之分殊矣物各賦物而不可
punctuated:
前後無非正人，出入起居罔非正道，則所見者正事，所聞者正言，所行者正道，而世子正矣。先儒曰：「太子正而天下定。」此天下之至言，萬世不可易之定論也。
天高地下，萬物散殊，而禮制行矣；流而不息，合同而化，而樂興焉。
李岫
同考試官教諭唐批：「有天地之和序，而後有禮樂之制作。作者往往認天地之和序為禮樂，失之矣。此篇獨得其大意，故表而出之。」
考試官左中允楊批：「講禮行樂興處最是。」
考試官右諭德王批：「體認親切。」
造化示自然之序，而禮所由制；造化示自然之和，而樂所由作。夫高下散殊者，天地自然之序；而周流同化者，天地自然之和也。孰謂禮樂之制作而有外於是哉？今夫天尊於上，地卑於下，一高一下，而兩儀之位定矣。大以成大，小以成小，有大有小，而萬物之分殊矣。物各賦物，而不可
translation_en:
…before and behind him there are none but upright men, and in his coming and going, rising and resting, nothing departs from the correct Way. Thus what he sees are upright deeds, what he hears are upright words, and what he practices is the correct Way; the heir apparent will then be upright. An earlier Confucian scholar said: “When the crown prince is upright, all under Heaven is secure.” These are supremely true words, a settled judgment that cannot be altered for ten thousand generations.
“Heaven is high and earth is low; the myriad things are dispersed and differentiated, and the institutions of ritual take effect. Their flow never ceases; they unite and transform, and music arises.”
Li Xiu
Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: “Only after Heaven and Earth possess harmony and order are ritual and music instituted. Writers often identify the harmony and order of Heaven and Earth with ritual and music themselves, and thus go astray. This essay alone grasps the essential meaning; therefore I have singled it out.”
Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: “The explanation of how ritual takes effect and music arises is particularly sound.”
Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Admonisher to the Heir Apparent: “The understanding is intimate and precise.”
The processes of creation reveal a spontaneous order, from which ritual is instituted; they reveal a spontaneous harmony, from which music is created. Height and lowness, dispersion and differentiation constitute the spontaneous order of Heaven and Earth; circulating flow, union, and transformation constitute their spontaneous harmony. Who could say that the institution of ritual and music lies outside these? Now Heaven is exalted above, and earth is lowly below. One is high and the other low, and thus the positions of the Two Powers are established. The great become great, and the small become small; there are great things and small things, and thus the distinctions among the myriad things are established. Each thing endows things [?], and cannot …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□□如此孰非天地自然之序乎人知其為
□□之序而不知禮之制也以之吾知其君臣
□賤之節文一天地高卑之差等親疎上下之
儀則一萬物散殊之次序與夫行諸朝廷施諸
鄉黨凡禮之秩然有序者一皆此序之自然也
則禮也者豈非天地之序乎地氣上躋天氣下
降周流於亭毒之表而無一時之止息天地訢
合陰陽相得槖籥乎化生之機而無一物之乖
戾絪縕化醇而不容以獨異如此孰非天地自
===
然之和乎人知其為天地之和而不知樂之興
也以之吾知其五聲六律之相宣無非絪縕之
氣之舒暢大小終始之相生無非化醇之氣之
宣泄與夫格於神人和於上下凡樂之純然無
乖者一皆此和之自然也則樂也者豈非天地
之和乎是知天地先禮樂而形禮樂後天地而
作聖人之禮樂天地之陰陽其相為流通者歟
故聖人始也法天地而為禮樂終也以禮樂而
賛天地所謂先天而天弗違後天而奉天時者
punctuated: □□如此，孰非天地自然之序乎？人知其為□□之序，而不知禮之制也以之。吾知其君臣□賤之節文，一天地高卑之差等；親疎上下之儀則，一萬物散殊之次序。與夫行諸朝廷，施諸鄉黨，凡禮之秩然有序者，一皆此序之自然也。則禮也者，豈非天地之序乎？地氣上躋，天氣下降，周流於亭毒之表，而無一時之止息；天地訢合，陰陽相得，槖籥乎化生之機，而無一物之乖戾。絪縕化醇，而不容以獨異。如此，孰非天地自然之和乎？人知其為天地之和，而不知樂之興也以之。吾知其五聲六律之相宣，無非絪縕之氣之舒暢；大小終始之相生，無非化醇之氣之宣泄。與夫格於神人，和於上下，凡樂之純然無乖者，一皆此和之自然也。則樂也者，豈非天地之和乎？是知天地先禮樂而形，禮樂後天地而作。聖人之禮樂，天地之陰陽，其相為流通者歟？故聖人始也法天地而為禮樂，終也以禮樂而賛天地。所謂先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時者
translation_en:
…[?] being thus, what is not part of the natural order of Heaven and Earth? People recognize it as the order of [?], yet do not recognize that ritual is fashioned on this basis. I understand that its articulated distinctions between ruler and minister, [the noble?] and the lowly, accord entirely with the gradations of height and depth in Heaven and Earth; its ceremonial rules for close and distant kin, superiors and inferiors, accord entirely with the ordering of the myriad things in their diverse stations. Moreover, in what is practiced at court and applied in village communities, everything in ritual that exhibits orderly arrangement derives wholly from the spontaneity of this order. Is ritual, then, not the order of Heaven and Earth?

The vital force of Earth rises, and the vital force of Heaven descends. They circulate throughout the realm of nurture, never ceasing for a moment. Heaven and Earth unite in harmony, yin and yang find mutual accord, working like bellows in the mechanism of transformation and generation, so that not a single thing is discordant. Intermingling, they transform things into fullness, allowing nothing to stand apart in isolation. Being thus, what is not part of the natural harmony of Heaven and Earth? People recognize it as the harmony of Heaven and Earth, yet do not recognize that music arises on this basis. I understand that the mutual resonance of the five notes and six pitch standards is wholly the free unfolding of intermingling vital forces; the mutual generation of greater and lesser tones, endings and beginnings, is wholly the release of the vital forces that bring transformation to fullness. Moreover, in reaching spirits and human beings and harmonizing superiors and inferiors, everything in music that is entirely free of discord derives wholly from the spontaneity of this harmony. Is music, then, not the harmony of Heaven and Earth?

From this we know that Heaven and Earth took form before ritual and music, and that ritual and music were created after Heaven and Earth. Are the ritual and music of the sages and the yin and yang of Heaven and Earth not mutually interconnected? Thus, at first the sages modeled themselves on Heaven and Earth to create ritual and music; ultimately, through ritual and music, they assisted Heaven and Earth. This is what is meant by preceding Heaven without Heaven going against them, and following Heaven while observing Heaven’s seasons…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也傳曰明則有禮樂幽則有鬼神噫必明於幽
而後可與言禮樂也
第貳場
論
君德以剛為主
孫清
同考試官教諭張批議論之文凡涉治道者便
容易下筆此題場中多善作者讀之初若可喜徐而
檢之則直泛論君德耳鮮有切題意者此篇有見識
===
有筆力有照應不出剛字立說而悠揚反覆機軸自
別毋乃空冀北之羣者乎
同考試官教諭李批遍閱論義動輒盈數
千言然皆騁浮辭耳於君德乎何關此論首尾開闔
委蛇曲折無一長語而寓有餘不盡之意於言辭之表
其善言君德者乎論場之冠無踰子矣
考試官左中允楊批近時作論者往往鍛鍊於
一字一句間以為古文至其命意處則疎矣所以形
之議論支離破碎殊無足觀如此作者何嘗不用時
punctuated:
也。傳曰：「明則有禮樂，幽則有鬼神。」噫！必明於幽，而後可與言禮樂也。

第貳場

論

君德以剛為主

孫清

同考試官教諭張批：議論之文，凡涉治道者，便容易下筆。此題場中多善作者，讀之初若可喜，徐而檢之，則直泛論君德耳，鮮有切題意者。此篇有見識，有筆力，有照應，不出剛字立說，而悠揚反覆，機軸自別，毋乃空冀北之羣者乎？

同考試官教諭李批：遍閱論義，動輒盈數千言，然皆騁浮辭耳，於君德乎何關？此論首尾開闔，委蛇曲折，無一長語，而寓有餘不盡之意於言辭之表，其善言君德者乎！論場之冠，無踰子矣。

考試官左中允楊批：近時作論者，往往鍛鍊於一字一句間，以為古文，至其命意處則疎矣。所以形之議論，支離破碎，殊無足觀。如此作者，何嘗不用時
translation_en:
…so it is. The Commentary says: “In the manifest realm there are rites and music; in the hidden realm there are ghosts and spirits.” Ah! Only when one understands the hidden realm can one discuss rites and music.

Second Session

Discourse

“The Ruler’s Virtue Takes Firmness as Its Governing Principle”

Sun Qing

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: In argumentative writing, any subject touching on the art of government readily lends itself to composition. Many candidates in this examination wrote well on this topic. At first reading their essays seemed pleasing, but closer examination showed that they merely discussed the ruler’s virtue in general; few addressed the precise purport of the topic. This essay displays insight, force of expression, and correspondence between its parts. Its argument never strays beyond the word “firmness,” yet develops expansively, returning repeatedly to its theme, with a distinctive organizing conception. Might this not be the one that empties the herds of northern Ji of their finest horses—that is, outshines all its rivals?

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: In reading through the discourses, I found that they frequently ran to several thousand words. Yet all merely indulged in empty rhetoric: what connection had they with the ruler’s virtue? From beginning to end, this discourse unfolds and draws together its argument, proceeding through graceful turns and winding developments, without a single superfluous word. Yet it conveys beyond its wording a wealth of meaning that remains unexhausted. Surely this is skillful discussion of the ruler’s virtue! For first place in the discourse session, no one surpasses you.

Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: Those who compose discourses nowadays often labor over individual words and phrases, supposing this to constitute ancient-style prose, while remaining careless about the conception of their argument. Consequently, the arguments they set forth are disjointed and fragmented, with virtually nothing worth reading. Has a writer such as this ever failed to employ contemporary…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
文體裕而明畧尓雅意味深長即拘拘模倣古人者亦
未能或之過也
考試官右諭德王批能說出剛為君德之主且
有一倡三歎之意要亦不為無見者錄之不特取其
文而已
論曰有至大之責者必本之至健之德可也責
任而極於天下之至大亦未易稱也而於此有
本焉本之於一身而達之於幾務施為之表主
之以一心而守之於羣居燕處之時一德純健
===
不詭於易溺之情而不奪於易移之物始乎健
終乎健如是而斷如是而守如是而蒞政臨民
則君天下之責始塞而君天下之德以成而凡
本之吾身以見之天下者固皆至健之德之所
流通而吾心之所主則又斷斷乎不易操而改
轍也東萊呂氏之言曰君德以剛為主嗚呼真
知言哉且君德果主乎剛否也吾不得而知也
君德不主乎剛否也吾亦不得而知也蓋嘗讀
易而得其說矣六畫純陽其卦曰乾而繫之者
punctuated:
文體，裕而明，畧尓雅，意味深長，即拘拘模倣古人者亦未能或之過也。
考試官右諭德王批：能說出剛為君德之主，且有一倡三歎之意，要亦不為無見者。錄之，不特取其文而已。
論曰：有至大之責者，必本之至健之德可也。責任而極於天下之至大，亦未易稱也，而於此有本焉。本之於一身，而達之於幾務施為之表；主之以一心，而守之於羣居燕處之時。一德純健，不詭於易溺之情，而不奪於易移之物。始乎健，終乎健，如是而斷，如是而守，如是而蒞政臨民，則君天下之責始塞，而君天下之德以成。而凡本之吾身以見之天下者，固皆至健之德之所流通，而吾心之所主，則又斷斷乎不易操而改轍也。東萊呂氏之言曰：「君德以剛為主。」嗚呼，真知言哉！且君德果主乎剛否也，吾不得而知也；君德不主乎剛否也，吾亦不得而知也。蓋嘗讀《易》而得其說矣。六畫純陽，其卦曰乾，而繫之者
translation_en:
…the contemporary prose style: expansive yet clear, concise and elegant [?], with profound and enduring significance. Even those who scrupulously imitate the ancients could scarcely surpass it.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Mentor: The writer succeeds in explaining that firmness is the governing principle of a ruler’s virtue; moreover, the essay has the resonance of one voice singing and three responding. In any case, its author is certainly not without insight. In recording it here, we value more than its literary qualities alone.
The discourse reads: One who bears the greatest responsibility must ground it in the utmost strength of virtue. When responsibility reaches the greatest extent under Heaven, it is no easy matter to meet it adequately. Yet there is a foundation for doing so. Root it in one’s own person and extend it into the outward conduct of affairs of state; govern it with a single mind and preserve it both in company and in private repose. Let this virtue be undivided and wholly strong, neither swerving under feelings in which one can easily become submerged nor overcome by external things that can easily sway one. Begin with strength and end with strength. Decide in this manner, hold fast in this manner, and administer government and oversee the people in this manner. Only then will the responsibility of ruling all under Heaven be fulfilled, and the virtue requisite to such rule be perfected. Everything rooted in my own person and manifested throughout the realm is indeed an expression of the flowing operation of this supremely strong virtue. What governs my mind, moreover, must remain steadfast, without changing its commitments or altering its course. Master Lü of Donglai said: “The ruler’s virtue takes firmness as its governing principle.” Ah, how truly discerning these words are! Whether the ruler’s virtue really takes firmness as its governing principle, I cannot know; whether the ruler’s virtue does not take firmness as its governing principle, I likewise cannot know. Yet I once read the Book of Changes and found the explanation there. With all six lines purely yang, the hexagram is called Qian, and the words appended to it are…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天行健君子以自強不息夫陽至於純則健
極於至矣而天以之行焉君之有德亦猶天之
有行也天以健而行君之德獨不以健而立哉
且人君以一身之微而總攝乎天下之大責之
固甚重而攻之者亦甚繁也國勢之維持人心
之齊集萬幾之先圖教化之作興夷狄之撫御
皆有責於人君而賴之以有成而又聲色之奉
日交于前淫巧之技日叢于外異端邪說日有
以蠱惑其聰明憸邪巧佞之徒先意逆志日伺
===
吾之便以求濟其私者又雜出而莫禦也是其
事幾之所叢委習染之所轉移非有剛以主於
其間則優游不斷將必至於頹敗委靡不可收
拾者矣故責之甚重勝之以有斷也攻之甚繁
勝之以有守也中立於甚重甚繁之間而一主
於剛以濟其斷以植其守不患其無寬厚長者
之心也而患其無發強剛毅之操不患其無包
含容納之量也而患其無紀綱體統之立不患
其無優柔豈弟之政也而患其無開闔操縱之
punctuated: 「天行健，君子以自強不息。」夫陽至於純，則健極於至矣，而天以之行焉。君之有德，亦猶天之有行也。天以健而行，君之德獨不以健而立哉？且人君以一身之微，而總攝乎天下之大，責之固甚重，而攻之者亦甚繁也。國勢之維持、人心之齊集、萬幾之先圖、教化之作興、夷狄之撫御，皆有責於人君，而賴之以有成。而又聲色之奉，日交于前；淫巧之技，日叢于外；異端邪說，日有以蠱惑其聰明；憸邪巧佞之徒，先意逆志，日伺吾之便以求濟其私者，又雜出而莫禦也。是其事幾之所叢委、習染之所轉移，非有剛以主於其間，則優游不斷，將必至於頹敗委靡不可收拾者矣。故責之甚重，勝之以有斷也；攻之甚繁，勝之以有守也。中立於甚重甚繁之間，而一主於剛，以濟其斷，以植其守。不患其無寬厚長者之心也，而患其無發強剛毅之操；不患其無包含容納之量也，而患其無紀綱體統之立；不患其無優柔豈弟之政也，而患其無開闔操縱之
translation_en: …“Heaven’s movement is vigorous; the noble man accordingly strengthens himself without cease.” When yang attains purity, vigor reaches its utmost perfection, and through it Heaven moves. A ruler’s possession of virtue is like Heaven’s possession of movement. If Heaven moves through vigor, can the ruler’s virtue alone be established without it? Moreover, the ruler, with his single, insignificant person, exercises overall control over the vast realm. His responsibilities are indeed exceedingly weighty, while the assaults upon him are exceedingly numerous. Maintaining the strength of the state, uniting the people’s hearts, planning ahead for the myriad affairs of government, promoting moral instruction, and pacifying and controlling the non-Chinese peoples—all impose responsibilities upon the ruler and depend upon him for their accomplishment. Yet offerings of music and sensual beauty daily crowd before him; extravagant and ingenious crafts daily proliferate around him; heterodox doctrines and pernicious teachings daily work to bewilder his understanding. Treacherous men and artful flatterers anticipate his wishes and divine his intentions, daily watching for an opening with him through which to advance their private interests. Such men arise on every side, with none to check them. Amid this accumulation of affairs requiring timely action, and these influences that alter him through habit and exposure, unless firmness governs within, he will drift indecisively and inevitably fall into ruin and enervation beyond recovery. Thus, exceedingly weighty responsibilities are mastered through decisiveness; exceedingly numerous assaults are mastered through steadfastness. Standing upright between these weighty responsibilities and numerous assaults, he must take firmness alone as his governing principle, to sustain his decisiveness and establish his steadfastness. The concern is not that he lacks the generous heart of a kindly elder, but that he lacks a forceful, firm, and resolute character; not that he lacks the capacity to embrace and accommodate others, but that he fails to establish governing discipline and institutional order; not that his government lacks gentleness and graciousness, but that he lacks, in opening and closing, holding fast and letting go…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
省察于虛靜之中以求其何者為剛而何者
非剛辨別於幾微之際以求其何者為剛之善
而何者非善體驗于推行之際以求其何者能
剛而何者則不能剛非無私不足以立剛之體
必將克去已私而後已非至正不足以致剛之
用必將守吾至正而後已非好尚之謹聽納之
公不足以為剛之助必將謹於好尚公於聽納
而後已如是則君德之剛成矣舉而措之則夫
事幾之所叢委即是以為應酬習染之所轉移
===
即是以為鎮定政必有所出權必有所歸其斷
也為英斷其守也為固守而至大之責可於是
乎少塞矣故聲色可欲也不足以易吾之介淫
巧可玩也不足以喪吾之德異端之說可喜也
不足以蠱吾之心志憸邪者不得以肆其詐巧
佞者不得以售其諛而先意以伺吾之便者又
無隙可乘而不得以濟其私見賢而必舉不為
慢也見不善而必退不為過也有功者必賞不
為僭也有罪者必刑不為濫也剛而有執維持
punctuated: 省察于虛靜之中，以求其何者為剛，而何者非剛；辨別於幾微之際，以求其何者為剛之善，而何者非善；體驗于推行之際，以求其何者能剛，而何者則不能剛。非無私不足以立剛之體，必將克去已私而後已；非至正不足以致剛之用，必將守吾至正而後已；非好尚之謹、聽納之公不足以為剛之助，必將謹於好尚、公於聽納而後已。如是，則君德之剛成矣。舉而措之，則夫事幾之所叢委，即是以為應酬；習染之所轉移，即是以為鎮定。政必有所出，權必有所歸，其斷也為英斷，其守也為固守，而至大之責可於是乎少塞矣。故聲色可欲也，不足以易吾之介；淫巧可玩也，不足以喪吾之德；異端之說可喜也，不足以蠱吾之心志。憸邪者不得以肆其詐，巧佞者不得以售其諛，而先意以伺吾之便者，又無隙可乘，而不得以濟其私。見賢而必舉，不為慢也；見不善而必退，不為過也；有功者必賞，不為僭也；有罪者必刑，不為濫也。剛而有執，維持
translation_en:
…Examine oneself in emptiness and stillness, seeking to discover what constitutes firmness and what does not; distinguish things at their most subtle beginnings, seeking to discover what is good in firmness and what is not; test it in practical application, seeking to discover where one can be firm and where one cannot. Since only selflessness can establish the substance of firmness, one must not rest until one has overcome selfish desires. Since only perfect rectitude can realize the functioning of firmness, one must persist in maintaining that rectitude. Since only caution in one's preferences and impartiality in receiving advice can support firmness, one must persist in being cautious in one's preferences and impartial in receiving advice. In this way, firmness in the ruler's virtue is achieved. When put into practice, it serves to respond to the pressing affairs that crowd upon him and to provide stability against the shifting influences of acquired habits. Government measures will assuredly have a source, and authority a place where it rests. His decisions will be discerning and decisive, and his resolve steadfast; thus his supreme responsibility may be fulfilled in some small measure.
Thus, though music and sensual beauty may be desirable, they cannot alter my integrity; though extravagant craftsmanship may offer amusement, it cannot destroy my virtue; though heterodox teachings may be pleasing, they cannot beguile my mind and purpose. The malicious and crooked will be unable to give free rein to their deceit, and clever flatterers will be unable to put their blandishments to use. Those who anticipate my wishes and watch for what suits my convenience will likewise find no opening to exploit and will be unable to advance their private interests. On seeing worthy men, I will invariably promote them, without negligence; on seeing those who are not good, I will invariably dismiss them, without error. Those with merit will invariably be rewarded, without exceeding what is due; those guilty of crimes will invariably be punished, without indiscriminate severity. Firm and holding fast to principle, in sustaining…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之方不爽也剛而能一齊集之化可成也剛而
能明萬幾之至微可裁决也剛以禦寇則神武不殺而
善治而教化可行也剛以禦寇則神武不殺而
夷狄可服也凡此皆剛之為也事之雜出于天
下而叢委于吾身者其責亦重矣其端亦繁矣
而吾之主之者固自有道舉之至易而不見其
難御之至簡而不見其繁人之望之如天之高
也可仰而不可攀如雷霆之震也可聞而不可
見如鬼神之靈也可畏而不可褻在我者常有
===
不可測之威而在人者常有不敢犯之志不動
而敬不言而信而事幾無不理習染無所移矣
於乎人君之為德是果主於剛邪抑不主於剛
邪智者當知所從違矣抑斯言也東萊之有感
於漢事而云然也在漢之時崔寔亦嘗言之矣
其言曰數世以来政多恩貸又曰刑罰者治亂
之藥石其意盖不滿於當時之事而欲復孝宣
之政以矯其弊是亦東萊之意也惜其說不及
東萊之純也然君德固主於剛矣要之亦豈可
punctuated:
之方不爽也。剛而能一，齊集之化可成也；剛而能明，萬幾之至微可裁决也；剛以禦寇，則神武不殺而善治，而教化可行也；剛以禦寇，則神武不殺而夷狄可服也。凡此皆剛之為也。事之雜出于天下而叢委于吾身者，其責亦重矣，其端亦繁矣。而吾之主之者，固自有道。舉之至易而不見其難，御之至簡而不見其繁。人之望之，如天之高也，可仰而不可攀；如雷霆之震也，可聞而不可見；如鬼神之靈也，可畏而不可褻。在我者常有不可測之威，而在人者常有不敢犯之志。不動而敬，不言而信，而事幾無不理，習染無所移矣。
於乎！人君之為德，是果主於剛邪？抑不主於剛邪？智者當知所從違矣。抑斯言也，東萊之有感於漢事而云然也。在漢之時，崔寔亦嘗言之矣。其言曰：「數世以来，政多恩貸。」又曰：「刑罰者，治亂之藥石。」其意盖不滿於當時之事，而欲復孝宣之政以矯其弊，是亦東萊之意也。惜其說不及東萊之純也。然君德固主於剛矣，要之亦豈可
translation_en:
…the methods of maintaining order will not go awry. With firmness and unity of purpose, the transforming influence that brings all into accord can be achieved; with firmness and discernment, even the subtlest matters among the myriad affairs of government can be decided. When firmness is used to repel invaders, divine martial power achieves good government without killing, and moral instruction can take effect [?]. When firmness is used to repel invaders, divine martial power subdues the peoples beyond the frontiers without killing. All these are the accomplishments of firmness. Affairs arise in profusion throughout the realm and pile up upon the ruler’s person: the responsibilities are indeed weighty, and their ramifications numerous. Yet there is assuredly a way by which I, as ruler, may preside over them. I undertake them with the utmost ease, finding no difficulty, and manage them with the utmost simplicity, finding no complexity. People look upon the ruler as upon the height of Heaven, which they can gaze up at but cannot scale; as upon the crash of thunder, which they can hear but cannot see; and as upon the numinous power of ghosts and spirits, which they can fear but cannot profane. In me there is always an unfathomable majesty; in others there is always a resolve not to venture to transgress. Without acting, I command respect; without speaking, I inspire trust. Thus no incipient affair remains unregulated, and ingrained habits cannot sway me.
Alas! Is the ruler’s virtue indeed grounded in firmness, or is it not? The wise should know what to follow and what to reject. Now, Donglai made this statement in response to the affairs of the Han dynasty. During the Han, Cui Shi also spoke of this. He said, “For several generations, government has abounded in favors and pardons.” He also said, “Punishments are the medicine and medicinal stones for curing disorder.” His intention, it seems, arose from dissatisfaction with the affairs of his day: he wished to restore the government of Emperor Xiaoxuan to remedy its defects. This was also Donglai’s intention. Regrettably, his argument did not attain the purity of Donglai’s. Yet although the ruler’s virtue is indeed grounded in firmness, ultimately how could it…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
以無制哉盖剛者義之德也一於義而不濟之
以仁未有不傷于刻者四凶决去三苗徂征舜
之剛也而好生之心未嘗忘戡黎伐密綱紀四
方文王之剛也而徽柔之德未嘗廢故孔子以
知仁勇三德為修身立政之要而司馬光進言
于其君亦有仁明武之說此則人君之全德而
春生秋肅在天之行亦有然者東萊之見非不
及此也而特為此言嗚呼其真有所感也夫其
亦有所警也夫
===
表
擬
賀
皇太子出閣講學表
孫清
同考試官教諭張批此善為四六者
同考試官教諭李批稱慶中寓忠愛之意
不獨其駢儷可取也
考試官左中允楊批表得體
punctuated:
以無制哉？盖剛者，義之德也。一於義而不濟之以仁，未有不傷于刻者。四凶决去，三苗徂征，舜之剛也，而好生之心未嘗忘；戡黎伐密，綱紀四方，文王之剛也，而徽柔之德未嘗廢。故孔子以知仁勇三德為修身立政之要，而司馬光進言于其君，亦有仁明武之說。此則人君之全德，而春生秋肅，在天之行亦有然者。東萊之見非不及此也，而特為此言。嗚呼！其真有所感也夫！其亦有所警也夫！

表

擬賀皇太子出閣講學表

孫清

同考試官教諭張批：此善為四六者。

同考試官教諭李批：稱慶中寓忠愛之意，不獨其駢儷可取也。

考試官左中允楊批：表得體。
translation_en:
…be allowed to remain without restraint? Firmness is, after all, the virtue of righteousness. When one devotes oneself exclusively to righteousness without tempering it with benevolence, one inevitably errs through harshness. Resolutely banishing the Four Malefactors and campaigning against the Sanmiao manifested Shun’s firmness; yet he never forgot his concern to preserve life. Subduing Li, attacking Mi, and bringing order to the four quarters manifested King Wen’s firmness; yet he never abandoned his virtue of gracious gentleness. Thus Confucius made the three virtues of wisdom, benevolence, and courage essential to cultivating oneself and establishing government. Sima Guang, too, in advising his sovereign, spoke of benevolence, discernment, and martial resolve. These constitute the complete virtue of a ruler. Heaven’s workings likewise show this pattern, bringing forth life in spring and imposing severity in autumn. Donglai’s understanding certainly encompassed this, yet he chose to make this particular statement. Alas! Surely something truly moved him to speak! Surely he also intended a warning!

Memorial

Draft Memorial Congratulating the Imperial Heir Apparent on Leaving the Inner Palace to Receive Instruction

By Sun Qing

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: This is the work of someone skilled in four-and-six prose.

Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: Within its congratulations it conveys loyalty and loving concern. Its parallel phrasing is not its only merit.

Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Companion to the Heir Apparent: The memorial observes the appropriate form.

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德王批典則
臣某等言弘治十一年月日伏奉
聖旨令
皇太子出閣講學者
學成日就
前星仰
光被之華
德本
淵微
===
少海衍流長之慶創壇畤之盛事成曠古之
偉觀臣等懽忭懽忭頓首頓首竊以洊雷
啓修省之誠繼照端化成之本事傳往昔
教有明徵自夏以來于周益盛世子有出
入之訓太公為襁褓之師弦誦禮書備春
夏秋冬之學道丞充弼選左右前後之賢
樹休烈于當時流耿光于後世秦不師古
漢亦非彛衣冠偶見於從遊羽翼遂煩於
調護用智囊而為令開博望延賓陋儒
punctuated:
考試官右諭德王批：典則。
臣某等言：弘治十一年月日，伏奉聖旨，令皇太子出閣講學者。學成日就，前星仰光被之華；德本淵微，少海衍流長之慶。創壇畤之盛事，成曠古之偉觀。臣等懽忭懽忭，頓首頓首。竊以洊雷啓修省之誠，繼照端化成之本。事傳往昔，教有明徵。自夏以來，于周益盛。世子有出入之訓，太公為襁褓之師。弦誦禮書，備春夏秋冬之學；道丞充弼，選左右前後之賢。樹休烈于當時，流耿光于後世。秦不師古，漢亦非彛。衣冠偶見於從遊，羽翼遂煩於調護。用智囊而為令，開博望延賓。陋儒
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, Right Mentor, comments: “Classical and correct.”
We, your servants So-and-so and others, submit: On an unspecified day and month in the eleventh year of Hongzhi, we reverently received the imperial command directing the Heir Apparent to leave his inner quarters and begin formal instruction.
As his learning advances daily toward completion, the Foremost Star—the Heir Apparent—reverently receives the splendor of your far-reaching radiance. As the foundations of his virtue grow profound and subtle, the Lesser Sea—the Heir Apparent—extends the blessings of an enduring stream. You inaugurate a splendid undertaking at the ceremonial altars [?], creating a magnificent spectacle without precedent in antiquity. We, your servants, rejoice, rejoice, and bow our heads to the ground, bow our heads to the ground.
We humbly consider that successive thunder awakens sincerity in self-cultivation and self-examination, while succeeding light establishes the foundation of transforming the people through education. Accounts of these matters have come down from antiquity, and there is clear evidence of such instruction. Beginning with the Xia, it flourished still more under the Zhou. The heir received instruction in his departures and returns; the Grand Duke served as his tutor while he was still in swaddling clothes. Music and recitation, rites and writings provided a full course of study through spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Guides, assistants, attendants, and advisers were selected from worthy men to stand on his left and right, before and behind him. They established admirable achievements in their own day and transmitted their brilliant light to later generations.
The Qin did not take antiquity as its teacher, and the Han likewise departed from established norms. Men in official robes and caps were only occasionally seen among the prince’s companions, and the task of protecting and guiding him consequently fell to those who supported him like wings. The man called the “Bag of Wisdom” was appointed director of the prince’s household, and the Bowang residence was opened to receive guests. Shallow scholars …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
侈稽古之榮誦說無關於身教曲士獻奏
賦之語端方何取於師資館闢崇賢徒為
觀美記頒資善亦是空言試厯數於前聞
皆莫盛于
今日兹蓋伏遇
皇帝陛下膺期啓運
握紀御天
孝弟慈以教成于家
知仁勇之優入于聖
===
日新舊學遵
大訓于文華風動餘休播新聲于海宇
龍軒萃祉
鶴禁開祥早建
元良式培仁於豐水益隆
佑啓乃養正於蒙泉蓋聖雖本於生知而性
亦由於習貫方惟
岐嶷具見
機衡三至無愆每謹問
punctuated:
侈稽古之榮，誦說無關於身教；曲士獻奏賦之語，端方何取於師資？館闢崇賢，徒為觀美；記頒資善，亦是空言。試厯數於前聞，皆莫盛于今日。
兹蓋伏遇皇帝陛下，膺期啓運，握紀御天，孝弟慈以教成于家，知仁勇之優入于聖。日新舊學，遵大訓于文華；風動餘休，播新聲于海宇。龍軒萃祉，鶴禁開祥。早建元良，式培仁於豐水；益隆佑啓，乃養正於蒙泉。蓋聖雖本於生知，而性亦由於習貫。方惟岐嶷，具見機衡；三至無愆，每謹問
translation_en:
…vaunted the honor of studying antiquity, yet their recitations and explanations had no bearing on teaching through personal example. Narrow-minded scholars presented their compositions in rhapsody: what upright guidance could be gained from such teachers? Chongxian Hall was established merely for outward show; the record promulgated for Zishan Hall likewise amounted to empty words. If we enumerate the precedents handed down from earlier times, none matches the flourishing achievement of today.
We humbly recognize that Your Majesty the Emperor has answered the appointed time and inaugurated a glorious destiny, grasping the guiding principles and ruling under Heaven. Through filial devotion, brotherly respect, and parental kindness, you have perfected instruction within your household; through outstanding wisdom, benevolence, and courage, you have attained sagehood. Daily renewing your longstanding learning, you follow the great instructions in Wenhua Hall; your abundant blessings spread like the wind, carrying a new sound throughout the realm. Blessings gather about the imperial carriage, and auspicious signs unfold in the crown prince’s palace. You early established the heir apparent, thus nurturing benevolence beside the Feng River; increasingly providing protection and guidance, you cultivate rectitude at the spring beneath the mountain. For although sagehood is rooted in innate knowledge, character also develops through repeated practice. Even in his tender years, the crown prince already displays discerning judgment [?]. Never failing in his three daily visits, he is always scrupulous in asking …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
安之節
萬幾有暇動承隨事之箴
虎幄天開
鑾輿日煥道同
父子建官參翰苑之儒法効
祖宗直講用
經幃之彦嘉言日進
乾行豈替於十寒公輔時陪
晉接未分於隻日取人為善能自得師學以
===
成之
天縱多能於不限薄言觀者世知
邁德之不凡是將建不世之偉功而嗣無疆
之歴服也臣等見聞歡駭遭際異殊一脉
陽和無巳鷦鷯之轉舌百重私慶莫伸弁
雀之揚眉伏願克勤于邦克儉于家
詒燕世傳於典則庸言之信庸行之謹
見龍化溥於文明臣等無任瞻
天望
punctuated: 安之節，萬幾有暇，動承隨事之箴。虎幄天開，鑾輿日煥。道同父子，建官參翰苑之儒；法効祖宗，直講用經幃之彦。嘉言日進，乾行豈替於十寒；公輔時陪，晉接未分於隻日。取人為善，能自得師；學以成之，天縱多能於不限。薄言觀者，世知邁德之不凡，是將建不世之偉功，而嗣無疆之歴服也。臣等見聞歡駭，遭際異殊。一脉陽和，無巳鷦鷯之轉舌；百重私慶，莫伸弁雀之揚眉。伏願克勤于邦，克儉于家，詒燕世傳於典則；庸言之信，庸行之謹，見龍化溥於文明。臣等無任瞻天望
translation_en:
…the observance of asking after his well-being. In moments of leisure amid the myriad affairs of government, he continually receives admonitions suited to each occasion. The tiger-adorned canopy opens beneath Heaven; the imperial carriage shines ever more brightly. Following the Way shared by father and son, you establish posts drawing upon scholars of the Hanlin Academy; emulating the ancestral emperors, you appoint as lecturers outstanding men of the classical lecture chamber. Excellent counsel is presented daily: how could Heaven-like diligence falter through “ten days of cold”? High ministers attend from time to time, and reception in audience is not restricted to odd-numbered days [?]. Drawing upon others to cultivate goodness, he can find teachers for himself; through learning he brings his capacities to completion, his Heaven-bestowed talents knowing no bounds. Even those who merely observe [?] recognize the extraordinary excellence of his virtue. He will thus establish achievements unmatched in any age and inherit the imperial succession without end.

We, your servants, rejoice in astonishment at what we have seen and heard; the circumstances we have encountered are exceptionally fortunate. With this continuous current of springtime warmth, our wren-like tongues cannot cease their song; yet even a hundredfold measure of personal rejoicing cannot express the delight of our sparrow-like uplifted brows [?]. We humbly wish that you may be diligent in governing the realm and frugal in managing the household, transmitting lasting peace to future generations through exemplary rules; that you may be trustworthy in ordinary speech and circumspect in ordinary conduct, so that the transforming influence of the “dragon appearing in the field” may spread widely through your resplendent virtue. We, your servants, cannot contain our feelings as we gaze toward Heaven and look toward…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖激切屏營之至謹奉表稱
賀以
聞臣等懽忭懽忭頓首頓首謹言
第叁場
策五道
第一問
孫清
同考試官教諭張批
皇祖憂勤之意著之
===
祖訓首章真足以詒
聖子神孫億萬載燕翼之謀也此策乃能鋪張而揚厲之傳之萬世我
皇上為今日守成之
聖君將於是乎徵而
聖世作人之效亦將於子乎驗矣
同考試官教諭李批我
聖祖憂世之心雖未易形容而詒謀典則固天下之所傳誦者學者多
不能知之何耶此策歷歷陳之而又及於
今日之事若能仰窺
punctuated:
聖，激切屏營之至，謹奉表稱賀以聞。臣等懽忭懽忭，頓首頓首，謹言。
第叁場，策五道。第一問。孫清。
同考試官教諭張批：皇祖憂勤之意，著之《祖訓》首章，真足以詒聖子神孫億萬載燕翼之謀也。此策乃能鋪張而揚厲之，傳之萬世。我皇上為今日守成之聖君，將於是乎徵，而聖世作人之效，亦將於子乎驗矣。
同考試官教諭李批：我聖祖憂世之心，雖未易形容，而詒謀典則，固天下之所傳誦者。學者多不能知之，何耶？此策歷歷陳之，而又及於今日之事，若能仰窺
translation_en:
…toward Your Majesty, with the utmost fervor and reverent trepidation, we respectfully submit this memorial of congratulation for your hearing. Your servants rejoice, rejoice; we knock our heads to the ground, knock our heads to the ground, and respectfully present these words.
Third Session. Five Policy Questions. First Question. Sun Qing.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor: The imperial ancestor’s concern and diligence, expressed in the opening chapter of the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun), truly provide a plan securing peace for his sagely sons and divine grandsons for countless ages. This policy essay expansively sets forth and celebrates that purpose, transmitting it to all generations. Our emperor, the sagely ruler who now preserves the inherited achievement, will find corroboration here; and the success of this sagely age in nurturing talent will also be demonstrated in you.
Comment by Associate Examiner Li, Instructor: Although the concern of our sagely ancestor for the world is not easily described, the authoritative principles of the plans he bequeathed are certainly recited and praised throughout the realm. Why, then, do so many scholars fail to understand them? This policy essay sets them forth distinctly, one by one, and also addresses the affairs of the present day, as though able reverently to glimpse…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□字黙契之意者有是哉子大竒也
考試官左中允楊批五策皆善答往事則引其
凡而不盡其言時事則微其辭而必切於用首問尤能頌述
我
皇祖貽謀之善與
今日
聖天子法祖之心即此亦可表於人矣前場況復稱是主司得士如此良用
自慶
考試官右諭德王批五策皆氣昌詞偉事核理
該而
祖訓一篇又能窺見
今日
聖心黙契
皇祖不言之微意可謂善觀
聖人者塾校前二場俱非他卷所及京闈首選非子其誰貢之春官□□
揚
明命矣
論
punctuated:
□字黙契之意者，有是哉！子大竒也！

考試官左中允楊批：五策皆善。答往事，則引其凡而不盡其言；時事，則微其辭而必切於用。首問尤能頌述我皇祖貽謀之善與今日聖天子法祖之心，即此亦可表於人矣。前場況復稱是，主司得士如此，良用自慶。

考試官右諭德王批：五策皆氣昌詞偉，事核理該。而祖訓一篇，又能窺見今日聖心黙契皇祖不言之微意，可謂善觀聖人者。塾校前二場，俱非他卷所及。京闈首選，非子其誰？貢之春官，□□揚明命矣。

論
translation_en:
…the meaning of tacit accord in the □ character(s) [?]—is this indeed so! You are exceptionally remarkable!

Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Rectifier: All five policy essays are good. In answering about past events, you bring out their broad outlines without exhausting the subject in words; on contemporary affairs, your phrasing is subtle but invariably pertinent to practical application. Your answer to the first question is especially accomplished in praising and recounting the excellence of our imperial ancestor’s plans for posterity and the present sagely Son of Heaven’s resolve to follow his ancestor’s example. This alone could serve as a model for others. Moreover, your work in the earlier sessions matches this standard. Having obtained such a worthy candidate, we who preside over the examination have good reason to congratulate ourselves.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Right Adviser: All five policy essays display abundant vigor and magnificent diction; their treatment of facts is precise and their reasoning comprehensive. Moreover, the essay on the Ancestral Instructions perceives how the present emperor’s sagely mind accords tacitly with the subtle, unspoken intentions of our imperial ancestor. You may indeed be called one who understands how to discern a sage. Upon careful comparison [?], your work in the two preceding sessions likewise surpasses the other scripts. Who but you could be the first choice in the capital’s Provincial Examination? We shall recommend you to the Ministry of Rites, □□ to proclaim the illustrious mandate [?].

Discourse

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖人憂世之言足以垂萬世無窮之訓契
聖人憂世之心足以保萬世無疆之業夫聖人
之心憂天下之心也誦其言而能求其心
則知
前聖垂訓之意固有所左求其心而又能體驗
擴充於丁寧反覆之外則
後聖之所賴以保萬世無疆之業者豈有外於
是哉生雖不敏於我
聖祖之明訓盖嘗莊誦伏讀於藏脩之餘神遊
===
意想於言詞之外而有以窺見其一二矣
則又未嘗不竊嘆曰大哉
皇言所以為天地立心為生民立命為
聖子神孫開萬世太平之業者其在於茲乎請
因明問所及而陳其槩
聖祖之訓曰凡古帝王以天下為憂者惟創業
之君中興之主守成之賢君能之夫創業
中興則但曰君曰主而於守成獨曰賢君
者盖創業中興之主披荊棘冒鋒鏑間關
punctuated:
聖人憂世之言，足以垂萬世無窮之訓；契聖人憂世之心，足以保萬世無疆之業。夫聖人之心，憂天下之心也。誦其言而能求其心，則知前聖垂訓之意固有所左；求其心而又能體驗擴充於丁寧反覆之外，則後聖之所賴以保萬世無疆之業者，豈有外於是哉？生雖不敏，於我聖祖之明訓，盖嘗莊誦伏讀於藏脩之餘，神遊意想於言詞之外，而有以窺見其一二矣。則又未嘗不竊嘆曰：「大哉，皇言！所以為天地立心，為生民立命，為聖子神孫開萬世太平之業者，其在於茲乎！」請因明問所及而陳其槩。
聖祖之訓曰：「凡古帝王以天下為憂者，惟創業之君、中興之主、守成之賢君能之。」夫創業、中興則但曰君、曰主，而於守成獨曰賢君者，盖創業、中興之主，披荊棘，冒鋒鏑，間關
translation_en:
The words through which a sage expresses concern for the world suffice to bequeath inexhaustible instruction to ten thousand generations; to accord with the sage’s heart of concern for the world suffices to preserve an enduring imperial enterprise for ten thousand generations. The sage’s heart is a heart concerned for all under Heaven. If, in reciting his words, one can seek to understand his heart, one will recognize that the earlier sage had a definite purpose [?] in bequeathing his instructions. If, in seeking his heart, one can also put it into practice and extend it beyond his repeated earnest admonitions, could what a later sage relies upon to preserve that enduring enterprise for ten thousand generations lie outside this?
Though I, a student, am not quick of understanding, in the intervals of my secluded studies I have solemnly recited and reverently read the lucid instructions of our Sagely Ancestor. Letting my spirit roam and my thoughts reach beyond their wording, I have been able to glimpse something of their meaning. I have then never failed to sigh privately: “Great indeed are these imperial words! Is it not here that we find the means to establish a heart for Heaven and Earth, to establish a destiny for the people, and to inaugurate an enterprise of peace for ten thousand generations for his sagely sons and divine grandsons?” Allow me to set forth its broad outlines in response to the matters raised in your discerning question.
The Sagely Ancestor’s instructions say: “Among the emperors and kings of antiquity, only rulers who founded dynasties, sovereigns who restored them, and worthy rulers who preserved their inheritance were capable of taking all under Heaven as their concern.” For those who founded or restored dynasties, he says simply “rulers” or “sovereigns”; only for those who preserved their inheritance does he say “worthy rulers.” This is because sovereigns who founded or restored dynasties cleared away thorns and brambles, braved blades and arrowheads, and passed through hardships…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
百戰之餘勤苦數年之後而後天下始一
民心始服故其能以天下為憂者此固理
勢之必然也惟守成之君生長於深宮之
中繼體於承平之後自非有英明拔萃之
資其亦何以知祖業之艱難民情之疾苦
而能以天下為憂哉故於守成之君獨謂
之曰賢此有以見
聖祖窮極人情之言所以誘掖獎勸於
來嗣者至矣然而創業中興與守成之君其
===
所憂雖若有不同者而其心則未嘗不同
焉盖創業之君其所憂者在天下之亂憂
之所以撥其亂而反之治也守成之君其
所憂者在天下之治憂之所以保其治而
免於亂也漢之高帝光武唐之太宗宋之
太祖當天下之未定則其所憂者在項籍
在赤眉在建德世充在蜀漢契丹及夫天
下之既定則其所憂者在諸將之桀驁在
功臣之難馭在制度之未備在方鎮兵權
punctuated:
百戰之餘，勤苦數年之後，而後天下始一，民心始服。故其能以天下為憂者，此固理勢之必然也。惟守成之君，生長於深宮之中，繼體於承平之後，自非有英明拔萃之資，其亦何以知祖業之艱難、民情之疾苦，而能以天下為憂哉？故於守成之君，獨謂之曰賢。此有以見聖祖窮極人情之言，所以誘掖獎勸於來嗣者至矣。

然而創業、中興與守成之君，其所憂雖若有不同者，而其心則未嘗不同焉。盖創業之君，其所憂者在天下之亂，憂之所以撥其亂而反之治也；守成之君，其所憂者在天下之治，憂之所以保其治而免於亂也。漢之高帝、光武，唐之太宗，宋之太祖，當天下之未定，則其所憂者在項籍，在赤眉，在建德、世充，在蜀、漢、契丹。及夫天下之既定，則其所憂者在諸將之桀驁，在功臣之難馭，在制度之未備，在方鎮兵權
translation_en:
…only after a hundred battles and several years of toil did the realm at last become united and the people’s hearts submit. That such rulers could take the realm’s welfare as their concern was thus a necessary consequence of principle and circumstance. A ruler who preserves an inherited achievement, however, grows up deep within the palace and succeeds to the throne after a period of peace. Unless endowed with outstanding intelligence and discernment, how could he know the hardships of his ancestors’ undertaking or the sufferings of the people, and thus take the realm’s welfare as his concern? Hence it is specifically the ruler who preserves an inherited achievement who is called “worthy.” This shows that the sagely founder’s words, which fathom human feelings to their utmost depths, provide the fullest possible guidance and encouragement to his successors.

Nevertheless, although the concerns of rulers who found a dynasty, restore it, or preserve its achievements may seem different, their underlying purpose has never differed. A founding ruler is concerned about disorder in the realm: his concern is how to quell that disorder and restore good government. A ruler preserving inherited achievements is concerned about the realm’s good government: his concern is how to maintain it and avert disorder. For Gao Di and Guangwu of the Han, Taizong of the Tang, and Taizu of the Song, while the realm remained unsettled, their concerns were, respectively, Xiang Ji; the Red Eyebrows; Jiande and Shichong; and Shu, Han, and the Khitan. Once the realm had been settled, their concerns were, respectively, the unruliness of their generals, the difficulty of controlling meritorious officials, the incompleteness of institutions, and the military authority of regional military commands…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之未釋而漢之文帝在位二十三年雖海
内富庶幾致刑措而兢兢持盈之心無異於
開基之主宋之仁宗在位四十三年雖深
仁厚澤社稷是賴而遑遑保治之念無異
於草昧之初此創業中興守成之君所憂
雖若不同而其心則未嘗不同者盖如此
豈直泛然徒日戚戚而已邪我
朝
聖聖相承重熈累洽萬無可憂之事然以
===
聖祖之時與今日天下之事言之則固有不同
者盖
聖祖之憂天下未定何以一之胡俗亂華何以
革之綱常淪斁何以復之姦暴未戢何以
摧之獄訟煩滋何以著之律令制度未定
何以著之典章大臣何以待之羣臣何以
體之勳戚何以處之近習何以制之中國
何以安之外夷何以攘之凡天下之事無
一不身親為之思慮區畫而後始有一定
punctuated: 之未釋。而漢之文帝在位二十三年，雖海内富庶，幾致刑措，而兢兢持盈之心，無異於開基之主。宋之仁宗在位四十三年，雖深仁厚澤，社稷是賴，而遑遑保治之念，無異於草昧之初。此創業、中興、守成之君，所憂雖若不同，而其心則未嘗不同者，盖如此。豈直泛然徒日戚戚而已邪？我朝聖聖相承，重熈累洽，萬無可憂之事。然以聖祖之時與今日天下之事言之，則固有不同者。盖聖祖之憂：天下未定，何以一之？胡俗亂華，何以革之？綱常淪斁，何以復之？姦暴未戢，何以摧之？獄訟煩滋，何以著之律令？制度未定，何以著之典章？大臣何以待之？羣臣何以體之？勳戚何以處之？近習何以制之？中國何以安之？外夷何以攘之？凡天下之事，無一不身親為之思慮區畫，而後始有一定
translation_en:
…had not yet been relinquished by the regional military governors. Emperor Wen of the Han reigned for twenty-three years. Although the realm was prosperous and populous, and he nearly reached the point where punishments could be set aside, his vigilant concern to preserve that flourishing state was no different from that of a dynastic founder. Emperor Renzong of the Song reigned for forty-three years. Although the dynasty depended upon his profound benevolence and abundant beneficence, his anxious determination to preserve good government was no different from that of a ruler in the earliest, unsettled days. Thus, although the concerns of rulers who founded dynasties, restored them, or preserved their achievements might appear different, their underlying purpose was never different. Could this have been merely a matter of vaguely fretting day after day?
In our dynasty, sage rulers have succeeded one another, with ever-growing prosperity and harmony, and there is absolutely nothing that might occasion concern. Yet if we compare the affairs of the realm in the time of the Sagely Progenitor with those of today, there are indeed differences. The Sagely Progenitor's concerns were these: The realm was unsettled—how could he unite it? Non-Chinese customs had disrupted Chinese civilization—how could he reform them? The cardinal human relationships and constant moral norms had fallen into decay—how could he restore them? The treacherous and violent had not been restrained—how could he crush them? Litigation was burdensome and proliferating—how could he set down provisions for it in statutes and ordinances? Institutions were not yet settled—how could he establish them in authoritative regulations? How should he treat the great ministers? How should he show consideration for his ministers as a body? How should he assign places to meritorious servants and imperial relatives? How should he control his intimate attendants? How could he bring peace to the central realm? How could he repel foreign peoples? Of all the affairs of the realm, there was not one for which he did not personally deliberate and devise arrangements; only then did there begin to be a settled…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之制故其事甚難而其憂甚遠也今天下
賦稅竭於東南徭役疲於西北法
祖宗矣而百度之或未貞謹天戒矣而休徵之
或未至疑獄矜矣而刑措之效或未臻直
言容矣而敢諫之風或未勵文命敷矣而
四夷未盡来王年穀豐矣而百姓未盡安
樂此皆天下可憂之事亦足以為承平之
警戒而不能不上廑
宵旰惓惓之慮者此固我
===
聖天子安不忘危之盛心亦我
聖祖垂訓之意所望於
聖子神孫以保萬世無疆之業者端有在於此
也噫自非深惟
祖業之重誠知為君之難中心惻怛以天下之
憂為己憂者其亦何能舍身心宴安之樂
而從事於憂虞警惕之地如此哉此又
祖訓不言之微意欲使
聖子神孫思而自得之者夫能思
punctuated:
之制，故其事甚難，而其憂甚遠也。今天下賦稅竭於東南，徭役疲於西北。法祖宗矣，而百度之或未貞；謹天戒矣，而休徵之或未至；疑獄矜矣，而刑措之效或未臻；直言容矣，而敢諫之風或未勵；文命敷矣，而四夷未盡来王；年穀豐矣，而百姓未盡安樂。此皆天下可憂之事，亦足以為承平之警戒，而不能不上廑宵旰惓惓之慮者。此固我聖天子安不忘危之盛心，亦我聖祖垂訓之意，所望於聖子神孫以保萬世無疆之業者，端有在於此也。

噫！自非深惟祖業之重，誠知為君之難，中心惻怛，以天下之憂為己憂者，其亦何能舍身心宴安之樂，而從事於憂虞警惕之地如此哉？此又祖訓不言之微意，欲使聖子神孫思而自得之者。夫能思
translation_en:
…system of regulations. Thus his undertaking was exceedingly difficult, and his concerns reached far into the future. Today, taxation exhausts the southeast, and labor services weary the northwest. The ancestors are taken as models, yet the many institutions may still not be properly ordered; Heaven’s warnings are heeded with care, yet auspicious signs may still fail to appear. Compassion is shown in doubtful criminal cases, yet the ideal of leaving punishments unused may still not have been attained; frank speech is tolerated, yet the spirit of courageous remonstrance may still not have been encouraged. Civilizing commands have spread abroad, yet the peoples of the four quarters have not all come to acknowledge imperial rule; grain harvests are abundant, yet the common people do not all enjoy peace and happiness. These are all matters of concern for the realm, sufficient to serve as warnings in a time of lasting peace. They cannot but engage the tireless concern of His Majesty, who rises before dawn and eats late in attending to affairs. This is indeed the noble intention of our sagely Son of Heaven, who does not forget danger amid security. It is also the intent of the instructions bequeathed by our sagely founder: precisely here lies what he expected of his sagely sons and divine grandsons, that they might preserve the boundless imperial enterprise for ten thousand generations.

Alas! Unless one deeply considers the weight of the ancestral enterprise, truly understands the difficulty of being a ruler, and, with heartfelt compassion, takes the concerns of the realm as one’s own, how could one relinquish the pleasures of bodily and mental ease and devote oneself in this way to anxious vigilance? This, too, is the subtle, unspoken meaning of the Ancestral Instructions, which the founder wished his sagely sons and divine grandsons to ponder and grasp for themselves. Now, if one can reflect…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
訓之言則能以天下為憂矣能以天下為憂
則天下享其樂萬世享其樂而天命之所
以眷顧於我
後人者何有窮已哉克
祖訓之言則堯舜之道常行於天下而六經可
不必作也大哉
皇言草茅之臣何足以知之
第二問
彭釗
同考試官訓導司馬批善治出於真儒程
朱之論意正如此此策推明體用一源之意皆自程朱論議
中來必有學有識之士也允宜高薦
同考試官教授陳批善治與真儒本非二事發
問之意此卷得之而故實不遺文有警策末又欲以周公
孟子為準的其詞若誇然學者言志固當如是也取冠一經
以勵其進
考試官左中允楊批策問不欲以隱僻事傲諸生所
不知正欲觀其才識耳此數子之事夫人能知之折以周公孟子高
punctuated:
訓之言，則能以天下為憂矣。能以天下為憂，則天下享其樂，萬世享其樂，而天命之所以眷顧於我後人者，何有窮已哉！克祖訓之言，則堯舜之道常行於天下，而六經可不必作也。大哉，皇言！草茅之臣何足以知之！
第二問
彭釗
同考試官訓導司馬批：善治出於真儒，程朱之論意正如此。此策推明體用一源之意，皆自程朱論議中來，必有學有識之士也。允宜高薦。
同考試官教授陳批：善治與真儒本非二事。發問之意，此卷得之，而故實不遺，文有警策。末又欲以周公、孟子為準的，其詞若誇，然學者言志，固當如是也。取冠一經，以勵其進。
考試官左中允楊批：策問不欲以隱僻事傲諸生所不知，正欲觀其才識耳。此數子之事，夫人能知之，折以周公、孟子，高
translation_en:
…the words of the Instructions, then one can take the concerns of All-under-Heaven as one’s own. If one can do so, All-under-Heaven will enjoy the resulting happiness, and ten thousand generations will enjoy it. How, then, could Heaven’s mandate ever cease to favor us descendants? If one can fulfill the words of the Ancestral Instructions [?], the Way of Yao and Shun will constantly prevail throughout All-under-Heaven, and the Six Classics need not even have been composed. Great indeed are these imperial words! How could a humble servant from the countryside be adequate to comprehend them?
Second Question
Peng Zhao
Comment by Associate Examiner Sima, Assistant Instructor: Good government comes from true Confucian scholars: this is precisely the purport of the Cheng masters’ and Zhu Xi’s discussions. This policy essay elucidates the idea that substance and function have a single source, drawing throughout upon their discussions. Its author must be a man of learning and discernment. He certainly merits a high recommendation.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: Good government and true Confucian scholarship are fundamentally not two separate matters. This paper grasps the intent of the question, omits none of the historical precedents, and contains striking and incisive passages. At the end, the author further proposes taking the Duke of Zhou and Mengzi as his standards. His words may seem boastful, but when a scholar declares his aspirations, this is indeed how he ought to speak. Rank him first among the candidates in his Classic, to encourage his further progress.
Comment by Examiner Yang, Left Rectifier of the Heir Apparent: In posing a policy question, we do not wish to vaunt our knowledge of obscure matters unknown to the candidates; we wish simply to observe their ability and discernment. Anyone can know the deeds of these several men. Judging them against the Duke of Zhou and Mengzi, and elevating …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
一歸于學則未有若此篇之詳盡者
考試官右諭德王批能知周公孟子易地則皆然於答
是策也何有此意惟此策能道之
道不行者不足以為善治而治必本於道
道不明者不足以為真儒而道必本於學
治而至于周公治之盛也行道者也下此
則皆道其所道耳學而至于孟子學之至
也明道者也外此則皆學其所學耳程子
嘗謂周公沒百世無善治孟軻死千載無
===
真儒誠哉是言也執事發策舉以為問而
及于漢唐宋之諸子其為世道慮至深切
矣請試陳之周公孟子之道一而已矣行
之者為善治明之者為真儒時有先後位
有隱顯而其所學初不異也使周公居孟
子之地則必能為孟子之述作而斯道以
明使孟子居周公之位則亦能為周公之
經制而斯道以行是故周公之學于今雖
不能盡知然無逸之訓發天命之精微四
punctuated:
一歸于學，則未有若此篇之詳盡者。
考試官右諭德王批：能知周公、孟子易地則皆然，於答是策也何有？此意惟此策能道之。
道不行者，不足以為善治，而治必本於道；道不明者，不足以為真儒，而道必本於學。治而至于周公，治之盛也，行道者也；下此，則皆道其所道耳。學而至于孟子，學之至也，明道者也；外此，則皆學其所學耳。程子嘗謂：「周公沒，百世無善治；孟軻死，千載無真儒。」誠哉是言也！執事發策，舉以為問，而及于漢、唐、宋之諸子，其為世道慮至深切矣。請試陳之。周公、孟子之道，一而已矣。行之者為善治，明之者為真儒。時有先後，位有隱顯，而其所學初不異也。使周公居孟子之地，則必能為孟子之述作，而斯道以明；使孟子居周公之位，則亦能為周公之經制，而斯道以行。是故周公之學，于今雖不能盡知，然《無逸》之訓，發天命之精微，四
translation_en:
…tracing everything back to learning, no essay has been as exhaustive as this one.
Examiner Wang, Right Mentor, comments: If one understands that Zhou Gong and Mengzi would each have acted as the other did had they exchanged circumstances, what difficulty could there be in answering this policy question? This essay alone expresses that idea.
Where the Way is not put into practice, there can be no good government; government must be rooted in the Way. Where the Way is not elucidated, there can be no true Confucian scholars; understanding the Way must be rooted in learning. Government such as Zhou Gong’s represents government at its height: he put the Way into practice. Below this, men merely follow whatever they take to be the Way. Learning such as Mengzi’s represents learning at its utmost: he elucidated the Way. Apart from this, men merely study whatever they happen to study. Master Cheng once said: “After Zhou Gong passed away, there was no good government for a hundred generations; after Meng Ke died, there were no true Confucian scholars for a thousand years.” How true these words are! You, honored examiners, have cited them in setting this policy question and extended your inquiry to the various thinkers of the Han, Tang, and Song. Your concern for the moral condition of the world is profoundly earnest. Allow me to attempt an explanation.
The Way of Zhou Gong and Mengzi was one and the same. Those who practice it bring about good government; those who elucidate it are true Confucian scholars. They lived at different times, and their positions differed in obscurity or prominence, but what they learned was never different. Had Zhou Gong occupied Mengzi’s circumstances, he would surely have been capable of producing Mengzi’s writings, thereby elucidating this Way. Had Mengzi occupied Zhou Gong’s position, he too would have been capable of establishing Zhou Gong’s institutions, thereby putting this Way into practice. Thus, although we cannot now fully know Zhou Gong’s learning, the admonitions in Against Idleness (Wu yi) reveal the subtle profundities of Heaven’s Mandate, and the four …

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
事之思繼三王之心法一時禮樂之制作
教化之大行皆自聖學中来其學盖不止
百篇之朝讀而已也孟子之學當時雖不
得小試然井田之論據先王之成法班爵
之說得周公之遺意行仁政而王齊如反
手舉斯心而運天下于掌上皆自度其所
能為者言之非誇辭也自周公以後王迹
熄而春秋作縱横于戰國火于秦黄老于
漢佛于兩晉以下而彌文于唐宋之間一
===
時得君秉政者非無其人然皆随世以就
功名者耳是毋恠乎無善治也自孟子以
後異端起而大義乖學者以權謀為宗而
黜六經談者以虚蕩為辯而賤名檢行身
者以放濁為通而狹節信進仕者以苟得
為貴而鄙居正一時著書立言者非無其
人然皆擇之不精語之不詳者耳是毋惑
乎無真儒也其得君秉政者若公孫弘王
安石皆是也其著書立言者若揚雄韓愈
punctuated:
事之思，繼三王之心法；一時禮樂之制作，教化之大行，皆自聖學中来。其學盖不止百篇之朝讀而已也。孟子之學，當時雖不得小試，然井田之論，據先王之成法；班爵之說，得周公之遺意。行仁政而王齊，如反手；舉斯心而運天下于掌上，皆自度其所能為者言之，非誇辭也。
自周公以後，王迹熄而春秋作，縱横于戰國，火于秦，黄老于漢，佛于兩晉以下，而彌文于唐宋之間。一時得君秉政者，非無其人，然皆随世以就功名者耳，是毋恠乎無善治也。自孟子以後，異端起而大義乖，學者以權謀為宗而黜六經，談者以虚蕩為辯而賤名檢，行身者以放濁為通而狹節信，進仕者以苟得為貴而鄙居正。一時著書立言者，非無其人，然皆擇之不精、語之不詳者耳，是毋惑乎無真儒也。
其得君秉政者，若公孫弘、王安石，皆是也。其著書立言者，若揚雄、韓愈
translation_en:
…his reflection on these matters carried on the teaching of the mind transmitted by the Three Kings. The establishment of rites and music in his time and the widespread extension of moral instruction all arose from the learning of the sages. His learning surely amounted to more than merely reading the hundred chapters in the morning. Although Mengzi had no opportunity even to put his learning to a small test in his own day, his discussion of the well-field system rested on the established institutions of the former kings, and his account of the allocation of ranks captured the intentions handed down by the Duke of Zhou. To practice humane government and bring Qi to true kingship would be as easy as turning over one’s hand; to extend this heart would be to move the realm in one’s palm. These statements all expressed his own assessment of what he could accomplish; they were no idle boasts.
After the Duke of Zhou, the traces of true kingship faded, and the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed. Then came the arts of diplomatic alliances in the Warring States, the burning of books under Qin, the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi under Han, Buddhism from the two Jin dynasties onward, and increasingly elaborate formalism during Tang and Song. There were certainly men in those times who won their rulers’ confidence and wielded governmental power. Yet they merely followed the tendencies of their age to achieve distinction and fame. Thus it is no wonder that there was no good government. After Mengzi, heterodox teachings arose and the great principles were distorted. Scholars took expedient schemes as their guiding doctrine and rejected the Six Classics; disputants took empty, unrestrained discourse for eloquence and disdained reputation and proper conduct; those cultivating their personal conduct regarded licentiousness and impurity as broad-mindedness and deemed integrity and trustworthiness narrow; those entering official service prized gain by any means and despised adherence to rectitude. There were certainly men in those times who wrote books and established doctrines. Yet they were merely men whose discrimination was insufficiently exact and whose explanations were insufficiently thorough. Thus it is no puzzle that there were no true Confucian scholars.
Among those who won their rulers’ confidence and wielded governmental power, Gongsun Hong and Wang Anshi were both of this kind. Among those who wrote books and established doctrines, such men as Yang Xiong and Han Yu…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
皆是也上疏金馬稱說周公弘之議論亦
可取也然曲學之譏長者不免抑不知東
閣之開果有握髮吐哺之意否乎好古樂
道自比孟子雄之沉潛亦可尚也然投閣
之事君子羞稱抑不知新莽之仕果有萬
鍾不受之介否乎愈之跋邪詆異以扶孔
氏其道盖亦自比孟子者然感二鳥之光榮
嘆一飽之無時較之集義養氣之功何如
也安石之秉執周禮講求法度其志盖亦
===
竊慕周公者然仗人主之威行空言之教
比之關雎麟趾之化何如也大抵世運有
古今而人才因之為高下學術有深淺而
治道隨之為汙隆分而言之則行道者稱
善治明道者號真儒合而言之則有真儒
然後能致善治體用一源非二事也朱子
嘗謂秦漢而下無人知講學明理所以無
善治盖講學明理真儒之事也使諸子果
有講學之功則必知周公之所以為治者
punctuated:
皆是也。上疏金馬，稱說周公，弘之議論亦可取也。然曲學之譏，長者不免。抑不知東閣之開，果有握髮吐哺之意否乎？好古樂道，自比孟子，雄之沉潛亦可尚也。然投閣之事，君子羞稱。抑不知新莽之仕，果有萬鍾不受之介否乎？愈之跋邪詆異，以扶孔氏，其道盖亦自比孟子者。然感二鳥之光榮，嘆一飽之無時，較之集義養氣之功何如也？安石之秉執周禮，講求法度，其志盖亦竊慕周公者。然仗人主之威，行空言之教，比之關雎麟趾之化何如也？

大抵世運有古今，而人才因之為高下；學術有深淺，而治道隨之為汙隆。分而言之，則行道者稱善治，明道者號真儒；合而言之，則有真儒，然後能致善治。體用一源，非二事也。朱子嘗謂秦漢而下，無人知講學明理，所以無善治。盖講學明理，真儒之事也。使諸子果有講學之功，則必知周公之所以為治者
translation_en:
…were all such men. Submitting a memorial at the Golden Horse Gate and discoursing upon the Duke of Zhou, Gongsun Hong offered arguments that also had their merits. Yet his elders did not spare him the reproach of twisting learning. Indeed, one wonders whether, in opening his Eastern Pavilion to worthy men, he truly shared the intention of the Duke of Zhou, who would grasp his unbound hair or spit out his food to receive visitors without delay. Delighting in antiquity and taking pleasure in the Way, Yang Xiong compared himself to Mencius; his deep immersion in learning was also worthy of esteem. Yet gentlemen are ashamed to speak of his leap from the pavilion. Indeed, one wonders whether, in serving Wang Mang’s Xin dynasty, he truly possessed the integrity to refuse a salary of ten thousand measures of grain. Han Yu attacked depravity [?] and denounced heterodox teachings in support of Confucius; in his pursuit of the Way, he too evidently compared himself to Mencius. Yet he was moved by the glory enjoyed by the two birds and lamented that he could never obtain even one full meal. How does this compare with the achievement of accumulating righteousness and nurturing one’s vital force? Wang Anshi adhered to the Rites of Zhou and investigated laws and institutions; his ambition, too, was evidently to emulate the Duke of Zhou. Yet he relied on the ruler’s authority to impose teachings consisting of empty words. How does this compare with the moral transformation celebrated in “The Ospreys” and “The Qilin’s Hooves”?

Generally speaking, the fortunes of the world differ between antiquity and the present, and the caliber of human talent rises or falls accordingly; learning may be profound or shallow, and the quality of government declines or flourishes along with it. Considered separately, putting the Way into practice is called good government, and those who illuminate the Way are called true Confucians. Considered together, only when there are true Confucians can good government be achieved. Substance and function have a single source; they are not two separate matters. Master Zhu once said that from the Qin and Han onward, no one understood how to pursue learning and illuminate principle, and consequently there was no good government. Pursuing learning and illuminating principle are indeed the work of true Confucians. Had these men truly attained proficiency in pursuing learning, they would certainly have understood how the Duke of Zhou brought about good government…

title: 弘治十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
何如孟子之所以為學者何如决不為希
世取寵之事惑世誣民之學矣若董仲舒
與諸葛孔明程朱皆以儒者氣象許之至
論其講學明理之功則亦容有未盡者盖
仲舒天資粹美用意純篤王佐之才也而
其學未免惑于灾異就使得君行道亦未
必能致周公之治孔明心術正大舉措光
明三代之佐也而其學未免雜于申韓就
使久于其位亦未必能興禮樂之化故論
===
者往往惜仲舒之不得及于孔門孔明之
不得遊于洙泗政以其學之不純不見聖
人之大道故也以此觀之則知講學明理
之功其關繫治道有如此者真儒之效豈
曰小補之哉方今
聖人在上道學大明誦習於庠序者皆聖賢之
言張施于廟堂者皆聖賢之道草茅儒生
亦善治中之一民耳然栖栖一畝之宫而
游心千載之上久矣今日之所學他日之
punctuated:
何如，孟子之所以為學者何如，决不為希世取寵之事、惑世誣民之學矣。若董仲舒與諸葛孔明，程朱皆以儒者氣象許之。至論其講學明理之功，則亦容有未盡者。盖仲舒天資粹美，用意純篤，王佐之才也，而其學未免惑于灾異。就使得君行道，亦未必能致周公之治。孔明心術正大，舉措光明，三代之佐也，而其學未免雜于申韓。就使久于其位，亦未必能興禮樂之化。故論者往往惜仲舒之不得及于孔門、孔明之不得遊于洙泗，政以其學之不純，不見聖人之大道故也。以此觀之，則知講學明理之功，其關繫治道有如此者，真儒之效豈曰小補之哉！
方今聖人在上，道學大明，誦習於庠序者皆聖賢之言，張施于廟堂者皆聖賢之道。草茅儒生，亦善治中之一民耳。然栖栖一畝之宫，而游心千載之上久矣。今日之所學，他日之
translation_en:
…what the Duke of Zhou’s practice of government was like, and what Mencius’s pursuit of learning was like; they would certainly not have undertaken acts that catered to the age to win favor, or pursued learning that deluded the world and deceived the people. As for Dong Zhongshu and Zhuge Kongming, the Cheng masters and Zhu Xi alike credited them with the bearing of Confucian scholars. Yet in their efforts to investigate learning and understand principle, there may still have been shortcomings. Zhongshu possessed an innately pure and fine disposition, and his intentions were sincere and steadfast: he had the talent to assist a true king. Yet his learning was not free from misguided beliefs concerning calamities and anomalies. Even had he found a ruler who would let him put the Way into practice, he might not have achieved government like that of the Duke of Zhou. Kongming was upright and magnanimous in his thinking, and open and honorable in his actions: he was a minister worthy of the Three Dynasties. Yet his learning was not free from admixtures of the doctrines of Shen Buhai and Han Fei. Even had he remained long in office, he might not have brought about transformation through rites and music. Thus commentators have often regretted that Zhongshu could not study at the school of Confucius, and that Kongming could not pursue learning by the Zhu and Si rivers. This is precisely because their learning was impure and they did not perceive the great Way of the sages. Viewed in this light, the importance of investigating learning and understanding principle to the practice of government becomes clear. How could the contribution of a true Confucian be called a mere minor assistance!
At present, a sage occupies the throne, and the Learning of the Way shines brightly. What is recited and studied in the schools consists entirely of the words of sages and worthies; what is implemented at court consists entirely of their Way. I, a humble scholar out of office, am merely one of the people living under good government.
